item.content:encoded:
Ranking Every MLB Playoff Team's Projected 2026 Postseason Rotation
Pitching wins championships.
While that old adage still holds true, it has taken on a slightly different meaning in today's game, as teams need to successfully utilize their entire pitching staff to make a deep playoff run, rather than simply leaning on two or three starting pitchers to shoulder the load.
Still, a strong performance from the starting staff can give a team a major leg up. The Los Angeles Dodgers were the perfect example of that last October.
Ahead, we've ranked the playoff rotations of every postseason team. Which team's rotation is best positioned heading into the playoffs?
12. Houston Astros
1 of 12
RHP Hunter Brown (6-3, 3.26 ERA, 1.28 WHIP, 120 K, 102.0 IP)
RHP Hayden Wesneski (5-2, 3.50 ERA, 1.15 WHIP, 41 K, 54.0 IP)
RHP Peter Lambert (8-10, 3.87 ERA, 1.26 WHIP, 153 K, 153.2 IP)
RHP Ethan Pecko (1-0, 4.31 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, 21 K, 31.1 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Ronel Blanco, RHP Cristian Javier (out for ALWC)
The Astros have used 19 different starting pitchers this year while navigating a long list of injuries. The fact that reliever AJ Blubaugh ranks third on the team with 95.1 innings pitched speaks volumes.
Ace Hunter Brown was slowed by a shoulder strain in the first half of the season, but he has returned to form with a 3.11 ERA and 81 strikeouts in 66.2 innings since the All-Star break.
With Cristian Javier making an early exit from his start on Wednesday, the rotation behind Brown is entirely up in the air. Hayden Wesneski and Peter Lambert are both capable of tossing a quality start, but they are short on big-game experience and could also be susceptible to a quick hook, shifting the focus to a Houston bullpen that ranks 17th in the majors with a 4.09 ERA.
11. Chicago White Sox
2 of 12
RHP Sean Burke (10-7, 3.40 ERA, 1.20 WHIP, 178 K, 167.0 IP)
RHP Davis Martin (9-7, 3.84 ERA, 1.29 WHIP, 121 K, 145.1 IP)
RHP Erick Fedde (8-9, 3.83 ERA, 1.36 WHIP, 99 K, 141.0 IP)
LHP Anthony Kay (9-9, 4.53 ERA, 1.37 WHIP, 125 K, 153.0 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Luis Castillo, RHP David Sandlin
The White Sox rank 26th in starters' ERA (4.62) and 28th in quality starts (34), so the starting rotation is something they will need to figure out how to navigate in the postseason rather than a strength.
Sean Burke and Davis Martin have accounted for 21 of those 33 quality starts. They will be asked to chew up innings at the top of the rotation, while games outside of their starts will likely be an all-hands-on-deck situation.
Sean Newcomb (58 G, 6 GS, 3.17 ERA, 88.0 IP) and Grant Taylor (59 G, 4 GS, 2.30 ERA, 82.0 IP) are both capable of providing length out of the bullpen, while deadline pickup Luis Castillo has also been shifted to a relief role.
10. Chicago Cubs
3 of 12
LHP Shota Imanaga (11-10, 3.74 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 171 K, 173.1 IP)
RHP Kevin Gausman (4-2, 4.83 ERA, 1.23 WHIP, 57 K, 50.1 IP)
LHP Matthew Boyd (10-5, 3.91 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, 96 K, 126.2 IP)
LHP David Peterson (6-2, 3.94 ERA, 1.39 WHIP, 68 K, 75.1 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Clay Holmes, RHP Javier Assad
The Cubs roll into October with arguably the best offense and best defense in baseball, but questions about their pitching staff hang over their postseason outlook.
Shota Imanaga has a 1.96 ERA and a 23-to-2 strikeout-to-walk ratio over 23 innings in September. That should put him in line to be the ace of the staff in October.
Veteran Kevin Gausman's significant playoff experience, including starting Game 2 and Game 6 of the World Series a year ago, should earn him a prominent role in the playoffs. At the back of the staff, Clay Holmes is the obvious candidate to shift to the bullpen given his past experience closing games.
9. San Diego Padres
4 of 12
RHP Michael King (12-10, 3.21 ERA, 1.18 WHIP, 159 K, 185.0 IP)
RHP Nick Pivetta (3-2, 2.86 ERA, 1.01 WHIP, 42 K, 34.2 IP)
RHP Walker Buehler (9-6, 4.56 ERA, 1.34 WHIP, 128 K, 150.0 IP)
LHP Robbie Ray (3-2, 5.02 ERA, 1.54 WHIP, 33 K, 43.0 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Casey Mize, RHP Randy Vásquez
The Padres rank fourth in the majors and top among projected playoff teams with 666.0 innings of work from their bullpen. That relief corps, anchored by Mason Miller and Adrian Morejón, will be a major factor in October.
Michael King is the clear ace of the staff. Nick Pivetta has pitched well since returning on Sept. 7, with 11 hits and three earned runs allowed in 14 innings over three starts.
Behind them, Walker Buehler is the logical Game 3 candidate, given his postseason resume and 3.15 ERA over 45.2 innings in his last nine starts. Deadline pickups Robbie Ray and Casey Mize have struggled since coming to San Diego and could be X-factors if they advance beyond the Wild Card Round.
8. Cleveland Guardians
5 of 12
RHP Gavin Williams (14-8, 3.63 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, 244 K, 181.0 IP)
LHP Parker Messick (12-9, 2.55 ERA, 1.04 WHIP, 191 K, 183.1 IP)
RHP Tanner Bibee (6-15, 4.35 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, 142 K, 182.0 IP)
LHP Joey Cantillo (11-9, 3.62 ERA, 1.42 WHIP, 171 K, 159.0 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Foster Griffin
Gavin Williams leads the AL with 244 strikeouts and Parker Messick has a 2.27 ERA in 71.1 innings since the All-Star break, giving the Guardians a legitimate one-two punch to lead the way in the postseason.
Opening Day starter Tanner Bibee has struggled, posting an 8.24 ERA over 19.2 innings in September, but his track record still makes him the most likely candidate to start Game 3.
The question then becomes who gets the nod between Foster Griffin and Joey Cantillo. Griffin has a 5.19 ERA in nine starts since he was acquired at the trade deadline, while Cantillo has better surface-level results but has issued an AL-leading 81 walks in 159 innings.
7. Atlanta Braves
6 of 12
LHP Chris Sale (14-9, 2.16 ERA, 0.98 WHIP, 200 K, 162.2 IP)
RHP Tyler Mahle (4-1, 1.99 ERA, 0.96 WHIP, 48 K, 54.1 IP)
RHP Grant Holmes (10-5, 3.47 ERA, 1.30 WHIP, 114 K, 147.2 IP)
RHP JR Ritchie (1-4, 4.79 ERA, 1.46 WHIP, 66 K, 67.2 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Bryce Elder, RHP AJ Smith-Shawver, LHP Martín Pérez (out for NLWC)
Starting pitching was expected to be a glaring issue for the Braves when Spencer Strider, Spencer Schwellenbach, Hurston Waldrep and AJ Smith-Shawver all began the season on the injured list.
Instead, Chris Sale has put together a Cy Young-caliber season, while journeyman veterans Martín Pérez and Grant Holmes have combined for a 3.26 ERA in 289.2 innings spanning 55 starts. However, Pérez was just placed on the injured list with lower back inflammation, making a bullpen game the likely approach to fill the fourth starter role if they advance to the NLDS.
Deadline pickup Tyler Mahle has given them the No. 2 starter they still lacked, while a healthy Bryce Elder could be an X-factor if they advance deeper into October.
6. Milwaukee Brewers
7 of 12
RHP Jacob Misiorowski (15-5, 1.86 ERA, 0.80 WHIP, 247 K, 169.1 IP)
RHP Logan Henderson (11-3, 2.47 ERA, 0.84 WHIP, 110 K, 98.1 IP)
LHP Robert Gasser (5-5, 4.01 ERA, 1.24 WHIP, 94 K, 103.1 IP)
RHP Dustin May (2-2, 5.61 ERA, 1.43 WHIP, 33 K, 33.2 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Kyle Harrison, LHP Shane Drohan
Jacob Misiorowski pitched out of the bullpen for the Brewers last October, posting a 1.50 ERA, 0.83 WHIP and 16 strikeouts in 12 innings across three appearances. He is now poised to lead their staff this postseason.
Rookie Logan Henderson has not allowed more than three earned runs in any of his 18 starts this season. He is 8-2 with a 2.19 ERA and 0.79 WHIP in 70 innings since the All-Star break.
Left-hander Robert Gasser has a 1.71 ERA in 26.1 innings over his last five appearances. He will be a significant part of manager Pat Murphy's plan of mixing and matching innings behind Misiorowski and Henderson.
5. Boston Red Sox
8 of 12
RHP Sonny Gray (18-5, 2.72 ERA, 1.15 WHIP, 149 K, 169.0 IP)
LHP Ranger Suarez (8-5, 3.22 ERA, 1.19 WHIP, 140 K, 148.1 IP)
LHP Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.03 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 171 K, 148.2 IP)
RHP Brayan Bello (6-7, 4.49 ERA, 1.37 WHIP, 90 K, 112.1 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Jake Bennett, LHP Patrick Sandoval
Few offseason additions have made a bigger impact than Sonny Gray, who has 20 quality starts in 29 games this year and is on track for his fourth career top-10 finish in Cy Young voting for four different teams.
Rookie Payton Tolle has been the team's most consistent starter behind Gray this year and will factor into the playoff rotation, while high-priced offseason signing Ranger Suarez has a 1.09 ERA over 24.2 innings in September.
The X-factor could be Brayan Bello after he threw a gem (8.0 IP, 5 H, 1 ER, 11 K) on the road against the Rays on Sept. 19. He has a 2.28 ERA over 51.1 innings while working mostly out of the bullpen since returning from a minor league demotion before the All-Star break, but he is stretched back out to start.
4. Tampa Bay Rays
9 of 12
RHP Drew Rasmussen (16-5, 2.67 ERA, 0.91 WHIP, 174 K, 172.0 IP)
RHP Nick Martinez (15-5, 2.94 ERA, 1.07 WHIP, 108 K, 177.1 IP)
RHP Freddy Peralta (4-2, 3.60 ERA, 0.98 WHIP, 39 K, 50.0 IP)
RHP Griffin Jax (8-10, 3.62 ERA, 1.19 WHIP, 115 K, 109.1 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Ian Seymour, LHP Shane McClanahan (out for ALDS)
Few organizations do a better job fully utilizing the entire pitching staff than the Rays, but this October they have three legitimate rotation anchors who can get them deep into games in Drew Rasmussen, Nick Martinez and deadline pickup Freddy Peralta.
That group gets even deeper if Shane McClanahan returns to action, though he has already been ruled out for the ALDS. Even if he's not able to return, reliever-turned-starter Griffin Jax has also been quietly excellent this season with a 3.23 ERA and 105 strikeouts in 100.1 innings over his 22 starts.
They could still opt to utilize an opener when it makes sense, or piggyback one of their starters with left-hander Ian Seymour if the situation arises. This isn't a staff that needs to lean on multiple bullpen games to get through a series.
3. Philadelphia Phillies
10 of 12
LHP Cristopher Sánchez (18-6, 2.93 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, 221 K, 200.0 IP)
RHP Zack Wheeler (13-5, 3.06 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, 188 K, 156.0 IP)
RHP Aaron Nola (7-11, 4.54 ERA, 1.33 WHIP, 177 K, 174.1 IP)
LHP Jesús Luzardo (14-5, 2.87 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, 221 K, 178.2 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Andrew Painter
Jesús Luzardo played catch earlier this week as he works his way back from shoulder inflammation, though his postseason status remains up in the air. There's a chance he will be limited to bullpen work early in the playoffs.
Veteran Aaron Nola has hit his stride of late, posting a 2.45 ERA in 66 innings over his last 11 starts, so he can fill the void behind the dynamic one-two punch of Cristopher Sánchez (7.7 WAR, 1st among all SP) and Zack Wheeler (5.6 WAR, 8th among all SP).
The Phillies rank second in the majors with 73 quality starts and 869.1 innings from their starting staff, so they are poised to lean on their starters as hard as anyone in October.
2. New York Yankees
11 of 12
RHP Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95 ERA, 0.92 WHIP, 239 K, 193.2 IP)
LHP Max Fried (5-5, 2.80 ERA, 0.99 WHIP, 104 K, 112.2 IP)
RHP Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 131 K, 127.0 IP)
LHP Carlos Rodón (7-3, 2.67 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, 91 K, 84.1 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Will Warren
With AL Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler and three established veteran starters capable of frontline production in Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón, the Yankees rotation is capable of making a major impact in October.
Schlittler logged a 1.26 ERA over 14.1 innings last October, including eight scoreless frames against the rival Red Sox in the Wild Card Round. He will now be asked to shoulder a heavier load.
It remains to be seen who the odd-man out would be in a series that calls for a three-man staff, though Rodón has made his case with a 1.42 ERA, 0.75 WHIP and 28 strikeouts in 25.1 innings in September.
1. Los Angeles Dodgers
12 of 12
RHP Yoshinobu Yamamoto (14-9, 2.53 ERA, 0.87 WHIP, 182 K, 185.0 IP)
LHP Tarik Skubal (4-2, 2.95 ERA, 1.13 WHIP, 60 K, 55.0 IP)
LHP Blake Snell (4-1, 1.86 ERA, 1.09 WHIP, 52 K, 38.2 IP)
RHP Tyler Glasnow (5-2, 3.53 ERA, 0.95 WHIP, 98 K, 74.0 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Emmet Sheehan, LHP Justin Wrobleski
The Dodgers have once again navigated much of the regular season without Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow, but they are healthy rolling into October and poised to round out the playoff rotation alongside Yoshinobu Yamamoto and deadline pickup Tarik Skubal.
The starting rotation logged a 2.68 ERA over 104 innings last postseason, with Yamamoto, Snell and Glasnow starting 13 of 17 games and the rest going to Shohei Ohtani, who will be limited to DH duties but has been sufficiently replaced by a two-time Cy Young winner in Skubal.
Right-hander Emmet Sheehan has a 0.53 ERA and 24 strikeouts over 17 innings in three September starts. He will serve as a multi-inning weapon out of the bullpen.

item.title: [sports.yahoo.com] Boston Red Sox Have Clear Offseason Need
item.dc:creator: Zach Coe
item.description: The Boston Red Sox offense delivered a disastrous performance in the Wild Card round of the playoffs, getting outscored 18-2 en route to a two-game sweep by the New York Yankees. After an anemic final month of the regular season, one thing is clear: the Red Sox must replace the power they traded away with Rafael Devers in 2025. In the Red Sox's four World Series wins since 2000, they have consistently been among baseball's best offenses. In 2004, they ranked first in runs (949), fifth in home ru
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox offense delivered a disastrous performance in the Wild Card round of the playoffs, getting outscored 18-2 en route to a two-game sweep by the New York Yankees. After an anemic final month of the regular season, one thing is clear: the Red Sox must replace the power they traded away with Rafael Devers in 2025.
In the Red Sox's four World Series wins since 2000, they have consistently been among baseball's best offenses. In 2004, they ranked first in runs (949), fifth in home runs (222), first in OPS (.832), and first in WRC+ plus (114). In 2007, they were fourth in runs (867), 18th in home runs (166), third in OPS (.806), and second in wRC+ (109). The theme continues in 2013, when they led the league in runs (853), were sixth in home runs (178), first in OPS (.795), and first in wRC+ (114). Finally, the 2018 Red Sox were first in runs (876), ninth in home runs (208), first in OPS (.792), and fourth in wRC+ (111).
Of course, for the first three World Series titles, Boston had Hall of Fame designated hitter David Ortiz in the lineup, and the 2018 team posted the best record in franchise history en route to a title. However, this trend isn't isolated to the Red Sox; over the last five years, each World Series-winning team (Dodgers, Rangers, Astros, Braves) ranked top 10 in those four categories.
The idea that power wins you games in the playoffs isn't new, and Red Sox Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow isn't unaware of it; it was among the first things he said at the 2025 GM Meetings. "I don't want to get so anchored to this idea that the only way to score runs is home runs. We showed that isn't the case. That said, a disproportionate number of runs in the postseason are scored via the home run, and that's not something that we can ignore," said Breslow.
The theory that runs are scored disproportionately via home runs played out in the Wild Card round against the Yankees, who scored nine of their 18 runs on home runs. The Red Sox themselves scored their only two runs of the series via a pair of solo home runs.
Yet, heading into 2026, the Red Sox offense clearly was a bat short, and that proved to be the case throughout the regular season as they finished the year 23rd in runs (689), 26th in home runs (163), 19th in OPS (717), and 17th in wRC+ (99).
A Rafael Devers-sized hole in the lineup
Unfortunately for Breslow and the Red Sox, a massive hole remains in the heart of the lineup where Devers once stood. In his first full season in San Francisco, the former Red Sox slugger hit .258/.340/.525/.865 with a career-high 37 home runs and 98 RBI on one of the worst teams in baseball. Adding Devers' home run total to Boston's would have vaulted them into the top 10 in baseball. Beyond providing a massive power boost to the Boston offense, Devers would also have stabilized the designated hitter spot, where the Red Sox got some of the worst production in baseball.
Devers also has a strong track record of success in the postseason, where he's hit .303/.382/.573/.955 with eight home runs in 26 games, and against the Yankees, against whom he posted .269/.346/.527/.873 in 122 games.
Regardless, Devers was traded, and he is not coming back. However, the team had to replace Devers' impact in the lineup, and ultimately they failed to do that. Willson Contreras had a career year in 2026, but he still profiles much more as a complementary piece to the guy in the lineup rather than being the guy himself.
Plenty of power options were available in free agency ahead of the 2026 season, including Pete Alonso, Kyle Schwarber, and even Alex Bregman. However, ultimately Breslow showed little interest in Schwarber, lost a bidding war to the Baltimore Orioles for Alonso, and was unwilling to include a no-trade clause in contract negotiations to retain Bregman. Instead, pivoting to building the team around strong pitching and defense.
Now that both pitching and defense are in place, Breslow needs to focus on adding power to the lineup because the overwhelming sample size shows that slugging leads to postseason success.

item.title: [heavy.com] Guardians' Nemesis Might Trade for Steven Kwan
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: Steven Kwan is going to have his name floating through trade rumors as soon as the Cleveland Guardians‘ season ends, and until he’s either moved, signs an extension, or the next season begins with him still on the roster. Really, Kwan has been in the rumors since the middle of the 2025 season. item.content:encoded:
Steven Kwan is going to have his name floating through trade rumors as soon as the Cleveland Guardians‘ season ends, and until he’s either moved, signs an extension, or the next season begins with him still on the roster.
Really, Kwan has been in the rumors since the middle of the 2025 season. The Guardians rarely keep players beyond their first six years of club control, and with that in mind, they often then trade them away to ensure they get some value rather than losing them in free agency for nothing.
Some rumors are more palatable for Cleveland supporters than others, though.
Because the latest trade idea involving Kwan would send him to the Chicago Cubs — the team that broke Cleveland’s hearts in the 2016 World Series.
Steven Kwan to Cubs?
Bleacher Report’s Kerry Miller included the Guardians trading Kwan to the Cubs as part of his new article on Monday examining “realistic” trades for the offseason.
He puts together the whole package, one that would have the Guardians sending Kwan to the Cubs for two prospects.
The two players Cleveland would get in return in this proposal are right-handed pitcher Jaxon Wiggins and utility man James Triantos. Both are former second-round picks who have yet to debut in the major leagues.
“On the prospects front, Jaxon Wiggins entered 2026 as a top 100 prospect on Baseball America, Baseball Prospectus and MLB, but he was a mess at Triple-A Iowa, walking nearly 20 percent of batters faced,” Miller writes. “Maybe Cleveland can fix his command, though, while James Triantos has .300 batting average, 30 stolen bases potential to replace Kwan.”
As far as player types, those guys both fit the Cleveland mold. The Guardians love to make pitchers better, and they certainly would enjoy a speedy contact guy like Triantos.
Dealing away Kwan would still be a tough pill to swallow for the Cleveland fanbase regardless.
Why Guardians Would Trade Steven Kwan
It all comes down to money in Cleveland.
When players get near the end of their contracts, the choice is either to extend them for more cash, or send them away for future value.
Aside from Jose Ramirez, the Guardians generally choose the latter approach.
“At any rate, two winters ago, they traded away the final five seasons of their seven-year contract with Andrés Giménez, and subsequently shipped Josh Naylor to Arizona, rather than paying what ended up being a $10.9M salary in his final year of arbitration eligibility,” Miller writes. “Despite their penny-pinching ways, they just keep making the postseason, winning the AL Central for the seventh time in 11 years. So, if they can turn one year of Kwan into a pair of former second-round picks, history suggests they probably will.”
Kwan is entering the final year of his contract. He’s arbitration-eligible for the final time and will probably get paid $10-11 million for 2027.
Whether it’s the Guardians paying him that or a different team is what this offseason will determine.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Chris Sale’s Bold Move Sets The Tone For Braves vs Dodgers NLDS
item.dc:creator: Greg Herring
item.description: The Ace Demands the Ball Chris Sale did not wait for a plan. He walked into Walt Weiss's office and demanded to pitch. This is the kind of guts that wins championships. Weiss admitted he would never have asked Sale to start Game 1 because he knew the pitcher would say yes even if he was tired. "First of all, I was not going to go to Chris Sale and ask him if he could pitch tonight," Weiss said after the Braves clinched their Wild Card series. The manager knew the risk but respected the fire. Sal
item.content:encoded:
The Ace Demands the Ball
Chris Sale did not wait for a plan. He walked into Walt Weiss's office and demanded to pitch. This is the kind of guts that wins championships. Weiss admitted he would never have asked Sale to start Game 1 because he knew the pitcher would say yes even if he was tired. "First of all, I was not going to go to Chris Sale and ask him if he could pitch tonight," Weiss said after the Braves clinched their Wild Card series. The manager knew the risk but respected the fire. Sale sat down and told Weiss, "I feel amazing." That simple line changed everything for Atlanta.
This move is not just about one game. It is about the mindset of a team that refuses to fold. Sale started Game 1 of the Wild Card series and finished the final four outs of Game 3. He is the first pitcher since himself in 2018 to do this. Weiss called him a warrior and said, "This guy — I've run out of superlatives for Chris Sale." The Dodgers have a stacked rotation, but Sale brings a level of intensity that money cannot buy. The Braves need this energy to survive the series.
The Rotation Puzzle
Atlanta's pitching depth is thin right now. Injuries have hurt the rotation badly. Tyler Mahle cannot pitch until Game 3 at the earliest. Martín Pérez has low back inflammation and has been ruled out for the entire NLDS. That leaves Grant Holmes and J.R. Ritchie as options. Holmes threw only two innings in the Wild Card win. A lefty reliever might even start as an opener. The Dodgers will start Tarik Skubai in Game 1. He is one of their aces and he has delivered several dominant postseasons performances.
Yamamoto tossed complete games in the NLCS and World Series last year. He closed out a winner-take-all Game 7 with zero days of rest. The stats show he is dangerous. He holds a .182 opponents' batting average which ranked third among qualified MLB pitchers. The Braves beat the Dodgers five times in the regular season, but the playoffs are different. L.A. is the defending back-to-back champion and they are rested. Atlanta had to play hard just to beat Philadelphia. The physical toll is real, but the mental edge belongs to Sale.
One Game To Win It All
The Braves must rely on their offense to keep this close. Michael Harris II hit a three-run homer in the first inning of the Wild Card clincher. Ozzie Albies and Matt Olson also hit home runs. Earlier this year, Yamamoto faced a leadoff home run from Drake Baldwin. That game ended 1-0 with the only run coming from Baldwin. If the Braves can score early, they can force Yamamoto into trouble. The Dodgers' three-peat bid starts this Saturday. The game time is 4 p.m. ET at Dodger Stadium.
Per MLB.com Braves, the broadcast will be on Fox, Fox Deportes, and FOX ONE. Triple-digit heat is forecast for Los Angeles, which could wear down pitchers late. The Braves have not made it past the Division Series since 2021. This series feels like a chance to break that cycle. Sale's boldness proves the team is ready to fight. The Dodgers have the stars, but the Braves have the heart. If Sale can get through the first few innings, the Braves have a real shot to steal this series. The clock starts Saturday afternoon.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] 2026 MLB Playoffs: ALDS, NLDS predictions and World Series picks
item.dc:creator: Rotoworld Staff
item.description: With the Wild Card round of the 2026 MLB Playoffs behind us, it's time for the Division Series to get underway. It all starts on Saturday with all four Division Series matchups. With that in mind, we polled the Rotoworld Baseball staff for their thoughts on how the rest of the postseason will play out. Check out our picks and analysis for the Division Series, Championship Series, and World Series. The 2026 MLB postseason has arrived. Stay up to date with the latest results and more. 2026 ALDS, N
item.content:encoded:
With the Wild Card round of the 2026 MLB Playoffs behind us, it's time for the Division Series to get underway. It all starts on Saturday with all four Division Series matchups.
With that in mind, we polled the Rotoworld Baseball staff for their thoughts on how the rest of the postseason will play out. Check out our picks and analysis for the Division Series, Championship Series, and World Series.
The 2026 MLB postseason has arrived. Stay up to date with the latest results and more.
2026 ALDS, NLDS Predictions
| Writer | White Sox vs. Guardians | Yankees vs. Rays | Braves vs. Dodgers | Padres vs. Brewers |
| Eric Samulski | Guardians | Yankees | Dodgers | Brewers |
| Matthew Pouliot | Guardians | Yankees | Dodgers | Brewers |
| David Shovein | Guardians | Rays | Dodgers | Brewers |
| Christopher Crawford | White Sox | Yankees | Dodgers | Padres |
| D.J. Short | Guardians | Yankees | Dodgers | Padres |
White Sox vs. Guardians
Crawford: I don't think there's much of a difference between the White Sox and the Guardians. I think the fact that the White Sox already won a pair of postseason games on the road, both relatively convincingly, is something working in their favor. I can't quite go team of destiny or any of that stuff, but there does seem to be something about this White Sox team. I realize that's not exactly the most scientific answer, but my heart believes in the Chicago Popes.
Yankees vs. Rays
Short: The Rays and Yankees are set to meet in the postseason for the second time ever, and the first with actual fans in the building. While the Rays were the better regular season team this year, I think the Yankees are better built for the postseason. It starts with the rotation, which was the best in the majors with a 3.30 ERA, but their bullpen was even better with a 3.15 ERA. Drew Rasmussen has dominated the Yankees in his career, but New York has a level of rotation depth the Rays simply can't match.
Aaron Judge's status for the ALDS remains uncertain because of his calf injury, but even without him, one could argue that the Yankees have the more dangerous lineup. Their ability to change the game with one swing is something I think will win out over Tampa Bay's small-ball style in a short series.
Braves vs. Dodgers
Pouliot: Atlanta's pitching staff received 7 2/3 innings from Chris Sale and seven from Tyler Mahle and still seemed hard-pressed to get through the three-game Wild Card series against the Phillies. How are they going to hold up without those two to start the series against the Dodgers? Even without the relief appearance Thursday, starting Sale in Game 2 would have required pitching him on four days' rest, which he hasn't done since early April. As is, it looks like Sale in Game 3 and Mahle in Game 4. Maybe the Dodgers' bats start off cold and the Braves can steal a game in Los Angeles, but as shorthanded as they are in terms of pitching depth, not having their rotation lined puts them at a major disadvantage.
Padres vs. Brewers
Samulski: The Padres have been red hot and dominated the Cubs, but I published an article before the postseason with research from the last 10 years that showed teams coming into the playoffs with tons of momentum don't meaningfully perform better than teams who struggle coming into the postseason. I might as well trust my own research. The Brewers have been arguably the best team in baseball all season. Their lineup is incredibly tough to get out, and they have possibly the deepest overall pitching staff in the postseason.
Full MLB Postseason Predictions
| Writer | ALCS Winner | NLCS Winner | World Series Champion |
| Eric Samulski | New York Yankees | Milwaukee Brewers | Milwaukee Brewers |
| Matthew Pouliot | New York Yankees | Los Angeles Dodgers | Los Angeles Dodgers |
| David Shovein | Tampa Bay Rays | Milwaukee Brewers | Tampa Bay Rays |
| Christopher Crawford | New York Yankees | San Diego Padres | San Diego Padres |
| D.J. Short | New York Yankees | San Diego Padres | New York Yankees |
Samulski: I will admit my bias again when talking about why I picked against the Yankees. I just think this Brewers team is finally going to break through. The Yankees were lights out against the Red Sox, but they have been prone to strikeouts throughout the season. That can make them a volatile offense, and I think the consistency of the Brewers will win the day here.
Pouliot: A few weeks ago, I might have picked another champ, but with the Dodgers' bullpen rounding into form, their biggest potential weakness seems gone. Edwin Díaz still isn't a sure thing, but he was much improved after coming off the IL, allowing just one hit and one walk while striking out nine in his final five innings. Roki Sasaki and Evan Phillips both hit 100 mph last week, and Kris Bubic, if he's even needed, could prove to be a secret weapon. Shohei Ohtani and Freddie Freeman might not be able to carry the offense at this point, but even if the Dodgers are lacking their usual firepower, they should be able to win some low-scoring games.
Crawford: I don't think the Padres are the best team in baseball. I don't think they're even the best team in their division. But I love the way they're playing now, and that bullpen, quality starters at the top of the rotation and just enough star power makes me believe they're built for the postseason, and their first-ever World Series championship.
Short: I love the Yankees' pitching and Aaron Judge should be back eventually in some capacity, which only improves the team's outlook for a potential World Series matchup. As opposed to their meeting in 1998, I would expect the Padres to make this one much more competitive. San Diego's offense has been great in the second half and their bullpen is positively scary. Still, the Yankees would hold the major edge in starting pitching, and that would ultimately make the difference in my hypothetical World Series matchup.

item.title: [heavy.com] Philles Predicted To Trade Bryce Harper — Back To Nationals
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: Bryce Harper and the Philadelphia Phillies have yet to win a World Series together. After another playoff elimination, it’s not clear that they ever will. And that at least begins to raise the question of a trade. It’d obviously be a gargantuan, bold move to trade Harper, but the Phillies are also coming toward a reckoning. They can’t keep doing the same thing and simply expect different results. If they were ever going to consider trading Harper, it’d be wise to do it sooner rather than later.
item.content:encoded:
Bryce Harper and the Philadelphia Phillies have yet to win a World Series together.
After another playoff elimination, it’s not clear that they ever will. And that at least begins to raise the question of a trade.
It’d obviously be a gargantuan, bold move to trade Harper, but the Phillies are also coming toward a reckoning. They can’t keep doing the same thing and simply expect different results.
If they were ever going to consider trading Harper, it’d be wise to do it sooner rather than later. He could return more value to Philadelphia that way.
And while if these rumors ever go anywhere, there will be plenty of potential suitors — but one would be way more interesting than any other: the Washington Nationals.
Bryce Harper Trade Prediction to Nationals
This thought came on social media from Chelsea Janes, who works for SNY now but used to cover MLB for the Washington Post.
If there’s anyone in the game who has information and also knows the Nats, it’s Janes.
This is what she wrote on X on Friday night:
“A thought I just had: Phillies need a revamp, will need to trade expensive stars, will require a trade partner with prospect capital, payroll space, and need for vet. Gen Z Nats are ready for a Werth-type, have prospect capital and payroll space to burn. Could you imagine…”
She’s referencing the impact Jayson Werth once made on the Nationals when he came aboard as a bearded veteran.
Yep, Harper would certainly feel quite a bit like that.
A thought I just had:
Phillies need a revamp, will need to trade expensive stars, will require a trade partner with prospect capital, payroll space, and need for vet.
Gen Z Nats are ready for a Werth-type, have prospect capital and payroll space to burn.
Could you imagine…
— Chelsea Janes (@chelsea_janes) October 3, 2026
Phillies Considerations
So if we assume that the Nats would want to trade for the 33-year old Harper, who is coming off a 29-homer season, then really all that matters is figuring out if the Phillies would do it.
He is signed through 2031, and he’s still owed about $125 million.
His contract will expire during his age-38 season.
That all adds up to a decision the Phillies need to make. Do they keep rolling with Harper, Kyle Schwarber and Trea Turner? Or do they change course?
The lockout may complicate things. It seems unlikely the Phillies would make any moves before the CBA expires on Dec. 1.
But that could give them more time to think. Is there interest in Harper, specifically from the Nationals? What would he cost? And are the Phillies really ready to alter their future this drastically?
If they are, a Harper return to the nation’s capital would certainly be fascinating.
He was drafted No. 1 by the Nats in the 2010 MLB Draft. He played seven seasons for Washington already. Why not some more?

item.title: [MLB.com] Braves-Dodgers NLDS Game 1 FAQ (4 p.m. ET, FOX/FOX One)

But since then, Atlanta has not made it past the Division Series round, while L.A. is the defending back-to-back champion. The Dodgers' three-peat bid will begin in earnest when they take on the Braves in the 2026 NL Division Series starting this Saturd
item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- The last time the Braves and Dodgers met in the postseason, a trip to the World Series was on the line.
The Braves ousted the Dodgers in the 2021 NL Championship Series, going on to win the fourth championship in franchise history. But since then, Atlanta has not made it past the Division Series round, while L.A. is the defending back-to-back champion.
The Dodgers' three-peat bid will begin in earnest when they take on the Braves in the 2026 NL Division Series starting this Saturday afternoon at Dodger Stadium, with triple-digit heat in the forecast.
During the regular season, the Braves outplayed the Dodgers, winning five of their six meetings and outscoring them 26-15. But the postseason is a different beast, and a rested L.A. club will meet an Atlanta team that had to play hard to eliminate Philadelphia from the best-of-three Wild Card Series.
When is the game and how can I watch it?
First pitch for Game 1 is set for 4 p.m. ET/1 p.m. PT on Saturday at Dodger Stadium. It will be broadcast on FOX, FOX Deportes and FOX ONE.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Braves: TBD
Injuries have depleted Atlanta's rotation. Chris Sale won’t be available before Game 2 on Sunday, and Tyler Mahle won’t be available before Game 3 on Tuesday. As for Martín Pérez, who was placed on the injured list with low back inflammation on Sept. 1, he couldn’t be activated before Game 3. Grant Holmes threw just two innings in Thursday’s win over the Phillies, so he may be asked to pitch the first few innings. Or, the Braves could go with Brent Suter as an opener and have Holmes follow.
Yamamoto had already established himself as a big-game pitcher long before arriving in the Majors, but he took it to another level last postseason when he tossed consecutive complete games in the NLCS and the World Series before closing out the winner-take-all Game 7 on zero days' rest. Yamamoto taking the ball in Game 1 would be the only way to have him available for a potential Game 5 on his usual rest.
What might the starting lineups look like?
Braves: Michael Harris II, Matt Olson and Drake Baldwin will have to contend with a lefty in Skubal again after facing two left-handed starters in Jesús Luzardo and Cristopher Sánchez during the Wild Card Series.
Dodgers: After Shohei Ohtani recovered from right biceps and left knee injuries and returned from the 15-day IL, manager Dave Roberts began using a platoon in the leadoff spot, slotting in Ohtani against right-handers and Mookie Betts against left-handers. The leadoff platoon, as well as other tweaks corresponding to the handedness of the opposing starter, is expected to continue in the postseason.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Braves: Didier Fuentes might be the only reliever who isn’t available. He pitched three consecutive days during the Wild Card Series. Robert Suarez has surrendered an extra-base hit in each of the three appearances he’s had since his right elbow inflammation forced him to the injured list in June. But his velocity was up and he looked more like himself while throwing two-thirds of an inning Thursday. He’ll likely get some high-leverage spots, especially with Dylan Lee struggling most of the second half and into the postseason.
Dodgers: L.A. may not have a set closer this postseason, but Tanner Scott, Roki Sasaki and Edwin Díaz all seem to be viable ninth-inning options. Righty reliever Edgardo Henriquez, whose regular season ended early due to a lower back strain, is expected to be activated for the NLDS as long as he comes out of bye week workouts feeling good, bolstering the Dodgers' already solid mix of leverage arms.
Any injuries of note?
Dodgers: Of the players who ended the season on the IL, the Dodgers are most confident about Henriquez returning. World Series hero Will Klein (right elbow discomfort) has faced hitters, but he has not pitched in a game since July 31 and is viewed as more of a depth option.
Who is hot and who is not?
Braves: Olson, Albies and Harris all homered in Thursday’s win over the Phillies. Harris went 5-for-11 in the Wild Card Series. Baldwin went 2-for-13 and Acuña was 1-for-9.
Dodgers: In September, Betts (1.112 OPS) and Teoscar Hernández (.965 OPS) were two of the Dodgers' hottest hitters. Tucker (.890 OPS) had his best month by far in his disappointing first season in L.A., perhaps getting hot at the right time.
Freeman dealt with right patellar tendinitis early last month, and he has slugged just .355 since the beginning of July. Ohtani recorded a .666 OPS in his past 29 games, when his biceps and knee injuries flared up and impacted his performance.
Anything else fans might want to know?
• The Dodgers are bidding for the fifth three-peat in World Series history, and the first since the 1998-2000 Yankees. They would be the first National League team to pull off the feat.
• The Braves and Dodgers will be meeting in the postseason for the sixth time. Atlanta was victorious in the 1996 NLDS and the 2021 NLCS. Los Angeles won the 2013 NLDS, 2018 NLDS and 2020 NLCS.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] What WAR Tells Us about the Dodgers' Postseason Prospects
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb
item.description: LOS ANGELES, CA — The Dodgers’ roster gives opposing managers plenty to worry about, and WAR helps explain why. It also gives Dodger fans a reason to appreciate players whose contributions can get overshadowed by the biggest names on the marquee. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES, CA — The Dodgers’ roster gives opposing managers plenty to worry about, and WAR helps explain why. It also gives Dodger fans a reason to appreciate players whose contributions can get overshadowed by the biggest names on the marquee. Put hitting, pitching, defense and baserunning on a common scale, and the picture becomes more interesting than a collection of home run totals and earned run averages.
MLB’s projected playoff rosters rank Milwaukee first (53.7 WAR), Los Angeles second (52.0); Dodgers free-agent acquisitions account for 24.5. That makes for an intriguing October argument: how much should we trust the accumulated value of a roster when the season becomes a succession of short series?
First, it helps to understand what the number actually means.
WAR stands for Wins Above Replacement. It estimates how many additional wins a player contributes compared with a readily available replacement, such as a minor league free agent. A four-WAR player has provided roughly four wins beyond that baseline over his playing time. The comparison uses a standardized replacement level, rather than whoever happens to be sitting on his team’s bench.
For position players, FanGraphs combines batting, baserunning and fielding contributions, expressed in runs. It adjusts for position, league and ballpark, incorporates the replacement-level baseline, and converts those runs into wins. Roughly speaking, about 10 additional runs are worth one win, although the conversion varies with the scoring environment. Position matters because filling a demanding defensive assignment carries value that a batting line alone cannot capture.
Pitchers require a different calculation. FanGraphs starts with Fielding Independent Pitching, emphasizing strikeouts, walks, hit batters and home runs, with an adjustment for infield flies. It accounts for ballpark, innings and the different roles of starters and relievers, then converts performance above replacement into wins. Relievers also receive a leverage adjustment reflecting the situations in which they pitch. Consequently, a pitcher’s ERA and his WAR can tell somewhat different stories.
These are FanGraphs figures, commonly called fWAR. Baseball-Reference uses a different calculation, particularly for pitchers, so its totals can differ. WAR is also an estimate: a few tenths of a win should never end an argument about which player is better.
Here are the Dodgers’ leading contributors on the FanGraphs leaderboard:
| Player | 2026 Dodgers WAR |
|---|---|
| Shohei Ohtani | 6.6 |
| Yoshinobu Yamamoto | 4.7 |
| Andy Pages | 4.5 |
| Max Muncy | 4.2 |
| Mookie Betts | 3.7 |
| Freddie Freeman | 2.7 |
| Tanner Scott | 2.4 |
| Tyler Glasnow | 2.4 |
| Tarik Skubal | 2.2 |
| Justin Wrobleski | 1.9 |
| Blake Snell | 1.9 |
FanGraphs figures through the regular season, accessed September 29. Skubal’s entry reflects his Dodgers work.
Ohtani’s total combines 3.7 WAR as a position player with 2.9 on the mound. Yamamoto supplied his value across 185 innings. Pages and Muncy both cleared four wins, an excellent reminder to give them their share of the credit. Scott’s placement alongside Glasnow is striking, too, given how much less opportunity relievers generally have to accumulate value.
For October, the workload details deserve attention: Glasnow accumulated his total in 74 innings, Snell in 42⅔ and Skubal in 62 for Los Angeles. Their season totals describe what they contributed over those opportunities; a postseason rotation presents a different distribution of innings.
That is where I find the strongest argument for the Dodgers. A playoff team can concentrate its innings among its best available pitchers. If those arms are healthy and effective, the version of a club taking the field in October can be considerably more dangerous than its season-long totals suggest. The same principle works in reverse when an important contributor is unavailable.
I would take the Dodgers’ combination of options into any series with confidence. Having several plausible game-changers gives a manager room to respond when an opponent neutralizes one part of the roster. It also gives the lineup a chance to survive a quiet series from a star.
Still, picking Los Angeles over any individual opponent is a different proposition from picking it over the entire field. Every additional round creates another opportunity for a brilliant opposing starter, a costly mistake or a badly timed slump to decide things. WAR can help establish expectations; October still gets to write the results.
For Dodger fans, these numbers support optimism and an appreciation of how many players have helped put the club in this position. The roster has enough talent to make a championship a reasonable expectation. Turning that expectation into another parade remains the most difficult part.
More Dodgers Coverage:
Have you subscribed to the Bleed Los Podcast YouTube channel? Be sure to ring the notification bell to watch player interviews, participate in shows & promotions, and stay up to date on all Dodgers news and rumors!
A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.title: [MLB.com] Forever connected by Braves, Olson and Freeman welcome first postseason faceoff
item.dc:creator: Mark Bowman
item.description: LOS ANGELES -- Freddie Freeman’s assumption that he would spend his entire career with Atlanta ended on March 14, 2022, the day the Braves acquired Matt Olson from the A’s. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- Freddie Freeman’s assumption that he would spend his entire career with Atlanta ended on March 14, 2022, the day the Braves acquired Matt Olson from the A’s. It was an awkward and initially painful separation for the man who had been the Braves’ everyday first baseman from 2011-2021.
Needless to say, the pain has faded as Freeman has spent the past five years establishing himself as a legend in another organization. He’ll always cherish his days with the Braves. But over this next week, they will stand as the enemy.
Freeman’s Dodgers will face the Braves in the National League Division Series that begins on Saturday at Dodger Stadium. The 2020 NL MVP has played 29 games against Atlanta over the past five seasons. But this marks the first time he will face his original organization in the postseason.
“I understand it will be a storyline,” Freeman said. “I get it. But it is five years later. I'm not going to try and look at it any differently. It's another team that I'm trying to get through to win another championship.”
The NLDS will create another opportunity to highlight the link that will forever exist between Freeman and Olson, the two players who have combined to provide the Braves excellence at first base over the past two decades.
Freeman certainly didn’t like seeing his job given to somebody else. As for Olson, it wasn’t easy for him to come to Atlanta to replace a franchise icon. But never once has there been any sort of animosity or awkwardness between the two first basemen.
In fact, the two have attended events together, including a Morgan Wallen concert at Truist Park last year. There is a genuine mutual respect.
“Matt is a great guy and an unbelievable baseball player,” Freeman said. “He's one of the best power hitters in our game right now. So it's fun. And he's from [Atlanta]. That massive home run he hit yesterday was just cool.”
Olson’s 416-foot home run in the seventh inning of Thursday’s night’s 6-2 win over the Phillies reminded the baseball world of his great power. Atlanta’s first baseman ranks fifth among all MLB players with 329 homers since the start of 2018, his first full big league season.
With the 41 homers hit this season, Olson joined Hank Aaron (eight times), Eddie Mathews (four times) and Ronald Acuña Jr. (twice) as the only players to tally multiple 40-homer seasons for the Braves.
“Matt had a lot on his plate when he first got here,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said. “He was replacing an icon. I think we got the only guy that could do it, the only guy that could step in in that role at that time. Matt's been a superstar for us.”
The Braves’ final written offer to Freeman was a five-year, $135 million deal ($27 million average annual value). The 10-time All-Star was 32 at the time.
The Braves knew Freeman might have a few more MVP-caliber seasons in him. But they also were confident Olson would provide similar production through those first few years and then continue to provide elite production while Freeman moved north of 35.
Of course, Freeman holds the edge in batting average (.306 to .259), OPS (.885 to .852) and most importantly World Series titles (2 to 0) over these past five seasons. He highlighted this run by becoming the only player in MLB history to hit a walk-off homer in a World Series game multiple times.
Olson is still bidding for that big postseason moment. But more importantly, he’s vying to lead the Braves to a World Series title, just like Freeman did in 2021.
“I’d say he’s our captain,” Braves catcher Sean Murphy said. “He goes out there every single day and hit 40 home runs. I’d say we’re happy to have Matt Olson on our team."

item.title: [Chicago Tribune] Column: Can the Chicago White Sox keep succeeding in the postseason without a conventional rotation?
item.dc:creator: Paul Sullivan
item.description: CLEVELAND — If you’re a baseball fan of a certain age, you’ve probably spent most of your life knowing some certainties about a pitching staff. item.content:encoded:
CLEVELAND — If you’re a baseball fan of a certain age, you’ve probably spent most of your life knowing some certainties about a pitching staff.
The five best guys (or four if you’re really old) are the starters who will try to get you through the bulk of the game. The best reliever is the closer, who pitches the last inning or possibly part of the eighth if he’s dominant enough. The next-best relievers — preferably one left-hander and one right-hander — are the setup men, the potential bridges from starter to closer.
And the pitcher who is least effective on the staff is the mop-up man, whose main function is keeping the better relievers from being overused.
For years managers used that basic blueprint, or something close to it, to get through the regular season. Then when the playoffs arrived, the best three or four starters went longer because the season was almost over and they could empty their bullets in the biggest games.
But baseball has changed, for better or worse, and now anything goes. Boston Red Sox ace Sonny Gray was removed in the fifth inning of a do-or-die wild-card game Wednesday, and Gray and his teammates grumbled about how the game got to this point.
Which brings us to the 2026 Chicago White Sox, who are trying to win with a “no-rotation” rotation.
Will Venable, the second-year White Sox manager, announced Friday that left-handed reliever Hagen Smith would start Game 1 of the American League Division Series against the Cleveland Guardians, serving as the opener Saturday, as he did in pitching three scoreless innings in Game 1 of the wild-card win in Houston.
It’s no surprise. The Sox have used openers a league-leading 32 times this season, including Smith’s outing Tuesday. If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it.
But does the no-rotation rotation have its limits, or can Venable’s Sox keep succeeding in the postseason with a bullpen-first strategy?
Venable acknowledged Sean Burke could start Game 2 on Monday, as he did in a four-inning start in Game 2 against the Astros, in which starters Anthony Kay and Erick Fedde both pitched in relief. But other than Burke, it might be a guessing game from here on out.
Can Smith come back to start Game 3 at home Wednesday, giving him three starts in their first five playoff games? Who knows what’s up Venable’s sleeve?
“I think the way it’s set up with these off days, we’re going to leverage the arms that we want to leverage when we want to use them throughout these first couple,” Venable said. “And if that means that one of the guys who we’ve been giving starts to throughout the season takes a bulk role in that, there’s certainly potential for that. But I think you can expect us to mix and match and use our best arms in the most optimal way.”
That suggests Smith and Grant Taylor can be the designated bookends of multiple games, with Jordan Hicks, David Sandlin and Sean Newcomb in the middle and Kay, Fedde and Davis Martin as the wild cards.
It’s almost the polar-opposite approach that then-manager Ozzie Guillén employed in the 2005 postseason, when José Contreras, Mark Buehrle, Freddy Garcia and Jon Garland combined for a 2.84 ERA in 12 starts, leading the Sox on an 11-1 run to their World Series title.
In the five-game win over the Anaheim Angels in the AL Championship Series, the four starters had four straight complete games and combined for 44 1/3 of the 45 total innings, with Neal Cotts contributing the other two outs in the ninth inning of the Game 1 loss. The rest of the bullpen had a nice seat to watch the starters dealing.
“I don’t know if you’ll ever see that again,” Sox catcher A.J. Pierzynski said afterward. “Managers just don’t do that anymore. They don’t have confidence to let guys go 120 pitches and throw nine innings.”
In the World Series, advance scout Bryan Little and his crew gave Guillén and pitching coach Don Cooper a near-perfect report on strengths and weaknesses of the Astros hitters. Contreras and Buerhle both went seven innings in the first two wins at Sox Park, and Garland went seven in Game 3 in Houston before the Astros tied it off Dustin Hermanson in the eighth.
Guillén was forced to use his well-rested bullpen when the game went 14 innings but also used Orlando “El Duque” Hernández and Buehrle. After Geoff Blum’s go-ahead home run in the 14th, Buehrle notched the infamous “buzzed save” by getting the final out after having a few beers in the clubhouse. “No more than three … I swear,” he later said.
Buehrle wound up on a Wheaties box, but he didn’t become a legend for his cereal-eating habits.
Game 4 was as old-school as it gets, with Garcia going seven shutout innings, Cliff Politte and Cotts getting the Sox through the eighth and Bobby Jenks closing out a 1-0 win to start the parade plans.
“That type of game is like the ones I watched for 162 games during the regular season,” Guillén said in the celebratory clubhouse.
Venable’s approach in the postseason also mirrors what he has done for much of the season.
General manager Chris Getz knew he didn’t have a dominant rotation in spring training, and opening-day starter Shane Smith was quickly dispatched to Triple-A Charlotte after three starts. Martin, Burke, Kay and Fedde have been the mainstays, though Fedde, who signed at the start of spring training, had only 15 starts in his 33 games.
Taylor has evolved into the de facto closer but can go three innings if needed. He also was used as an opener in April. Seranthony Domínguez led the team 12 saves, even after being dispatched at the trade deadline.
Openers aren’t a new concept. “Bullpenning” has been around for the last decade. Cubs manager Craig Counsell also used openers in last year’s postseason.
But is it possible no team has been as unconventional as the ’26 Sox in this particular run?
“It’s possible,” Getz said during the wild-card celebration. “We weren’t trying to re-create the wheel. We were trying to optimize the group that we had. So much of (baseball) has relied on starting pitching. We would’ve liked to do that. But if we were trying to win games, we had to lean on the strength of the club, and we’ve done that.”
The Sox’s strategy has been criticized, especially when an opener puts the bulk pitcher in a hole. Guillén himself has said on the Chicago Sports Network he’s not a fan of openers.
But if the Sox go all the way without a true rotation, the players may never have to buy a meal or drink in Chicago again. Or at least that’s the adage.
“More often than not I’ll just roll in and buy a drink or buy my dinner,” Blum told me last week in Houston. “But every so often, if there is a hard-core Sox fan in the bar or in the restaurant, there will be a free drink that will show up once in a while.”
So it’s kind of true?
“It still carries a little bit of weight,” Blum said. “We’re not quite the ’85 Bears, but the ’05 Sox do OK.”

item.title: [NESN] Red Sox-Yankees Made History, and It Shows MLB Can't Face a Lockout | NESN
item.dc:creator: Jon Conahan
item.description: The Boston Red Sox might not have played well against the New York Yankees, getting swept in the Wild Card round by their biggest rival, but the series still made some history. Whenever the Yankees and Red Sox play, especially in a playoff setting, it's typically action-packed, and fans watch from all over the world. The Yankees and Red Sox are such big rivals because both organizations have strong teams year in and year out and are also massive brands. According to the latest report, Game 1 bet
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox might not have played well against the New York Yankees, getting swept in the Wild Card round by their biggest rival, but the series still made some history.
Whenever the Yankees and Red Sox play, especially in a playoff setting, it's typically action-packed, and fans watch from all over the world.
The Yankees and Red Sox are such big rivals because both organizations have strong teams year in and year out and are also massive brands.
According to the latest report, Game 1 between the two squads actually set some records, making it the most-watched opener of an MLB Wild Card or Division Series since 2006.
“Tuesday’s Game 1 averaged 7.3 million viewers across NBC and Peacock, making it the most-watched opener of an MLB Wild Card or Division Series since 2006, according to Front Office Sports. The rivalry gave NBC Sports a strong start in its return to postseason baseball,” Chris Spiering wrote.
Baseball continues to rise at a rapid rate, a very promising sign considering the potential lockout this offseason.
That's something owners don't seem to be considering right now, and it has to change.
For baseball to keep growing, a lockout right when the game is growing at this level would be very questionable. Not to say that the Red Sox and Yankees aren't a big reason for that, but baseball has also seen some upticks in other viewership numbers, and possibly ruining that would be a very bad sign.

item.content:encoded:
For the Sixth Consecutive Year, TelevisaUnivision’s Sports Audio Network Will Deliver Live, Play-by-Play Coverage of the MLB Playoffs Through the 122nd World Series Across All Platforms.
Courtesy: TelevisaUnivision
MIAMI, FL. – October 2, 2026 – TUDN Radio, the premier Hispanic sports audio network of TelevisaUnivision, will once again serve as the exclusive U.S. Spanish-language radio home for the 2026 Major League Baseball Postseason. Marking the network’s sixth consecutive edition delivering October baseball to Hispanic audiences across the nation, fans can experience the entire postseason journey entirely in Spanish—from the opening pitch of the Wild Card Series through the final out of the historic 122nd World Series.
Continuing its long-standing collaboration with Major League Baseball, TUDN Radio will bring every moment of the postseason to life, led by the voices of acclaimed announcers Luis Quiñones, Alberto “El Beto” Ferreiro, Daniel Alvarez, and Jesus Acosta. This elite broadcast team will provide unparalleled coverage across the network’s nationwide terrestrial radio footprint, as well as digitally via the Uforia app and TUDN’s digital platforms.
“Baseball holds a deep, passionate connection with our Hispanic audience, and we are incredibly proud to return for our sixth postseason as the exclusive Spanish-language audio voice of MLB,” said Carlos F. Azcarate, VP of Sports Radio Network. “We are thrilled to continue bringing fans closer to the diamond, delivering every pivotal moment, dramatic home run, and championship celebration directly to them, wherever they choose to listen.”
Unprecedented Coverage Across All Platforms
TUDN Radio will broadcast key matchups throughout each round of the postseason, culminating in comprehensive Spanish-language audio coverage of the entire Fall Classic. Listeners can tune in across multiple touchpoints:
- TUDN Radio Network: Broadcast across affiliate radio stations in primary Hispanic markets nationwide.
- The Uforia App: TelevisaUnivision’s audio platform, offering live streaming on mobile devices across the United States.
- TUDN.com and TUDN App: Live digital audio integration for fans following games online.
- Smart Speakers & Connected Devices: Voice-activated live streaming through supported home integrations.
The 2026 Postseason Schedule on TUDN Radio
TUDN Radio’s coverage will feature full pre-game, play-by-play, and post-game analysis across every round:
- MLB Wild Card Series: Complete coverage of the best-of-three opening rounds.
- American League and National League Division Series (ALDS & NLDS): In-depth coverage as teams battle for the pennant.
- American League and National League Championship Series (ALCS & NLCS): Live calls deciding the champions of each league.
- The 122nd World Series: Uninterrupted, full-series coverage of baseball’s championship showdown.
Adding to the comprehensive live game broadcasts, fans can catch all the surrounding excitement, expert breakdowns, and exclusive player interviews on TUDN Radio’s premier baseball show, Desde El Diamante.
Complete broadcast schedules, station directories, and talent assignments will be updated throughout the month as matchups advance. Fans can follow along with live game updates, highlights, and behind-the-scenes content on X, Instagram, and Facebook via @TUDNRadio and by visiting TUDN.com.
CONTACT:
Melissa Agudelo – Director of Communications, News & Sports
###
TUDN Radio Regresa como la Casa Radial Exclusiva en Español en EE. UU. para la Postemporada de la MLB 2026
Por sexto año consecutivo, la cadena de audio deportivo de TelevisaUnivision ofrecerá cobertura en vivo, narración jugada a jugada y análisis de los Playoffs de la MLB hasta la 122.ª Serie Mundial en todas sus plataformas
Cortesía: TelevisaUnivision
MIAMI, Florida – 2 de octubre de 2026 – TUDN Radio, la principal cadena de audio deportivo para la audiencia hispana de TelevisaUnivision, volverá a ser la casa exclusiva de radio en español en EE. UU. de la Postemporada de las Grandes Ligas 2026. Por sexto año consecutivo, la cadena llevará el beisbol de octubre a las audiencias hispanas de todo el país, permitiéndoles vivir de principio a fin la emoción de la postemporada en español, desde el primer lanzamiento de la Serie de Comodines hasta el último out de la histórica 122.ª Serie Mundial.
Como parte de su colaboración de larga trayectoria con Major League Baseball, TUDN Radio llevará a los aficionados cada instante de la postemporada de la mano de los reconocidos narradores Luis Quiñones, Alberto “El Beto” Ferreiro, Daniel Alvarez y Jesús Acosta. Este destacado equipo de transmisión ofrecerá una cobertura de primer nivel a través de la red de estaciones de radio terrestre de la cadena en todo el país, así como en formato digital mediante la app de Uforia y las plataformas digitales de TUDN.
“El beisbol mantiene un vínculo profundo y apasionado con nuestra audiencia hispana, y nos llena de orgullo regresar por sexto año consecutivo como la voz exclusiva en español de la postemporada de la MLB”, afirmó Carlos F. Azcarate, VP de Sports Radio Network. “Nos entusiasma seguir acercando a los aficionados al diamante y llevarles cada momento decisivo, cada cuadrangular dramático y cada celebración del campeonato, sin importar dónde elijan escucharnos”.
Cobertura sin precedentes en todas las plataformas
TUDN Radio transmitirá los enfrentamientos más destacados de cada ronda de la postemporada, hasta llegar a una cobertura integral en audio en español de toda la Serie Mundial. Los aficionados podrán seguir la acción a través de múltiples plataformas:
- TUDN Radio Network: Transmisiones a través de estaciones afiliadas en los principales mercados hispanos de todo el país.
- La app de Uforia: La plataforma de audio de TelevisaUnivision ofrecerá streaming en vivo para dispositivos móviles en todo Estados Unidos.
- TUDN.com y la app de TUDN: Integración de audio digital en vivo para los aficionados que sigan los partidos por internet.
- Altavoces inteligentes y dispositivos conectados: Streaming en vivo mediante comandos de voz a través de las integraciones domésticas compatibles.
Calendario de la Postemporada 2026 en TUDN Radio
La cobertura de TUDN Radio incluirá previa, narración jugada a jugada y análisis posterior a cada encuentro durante todas las rondas de la postemporada:
- Serie de Comodines de la MLB: Cobertura completa de la ronda inaugural al mejor de tres juegos.

item.title: [Sportsnaut] MLB Insider Claims Phillies Will 'Kick Around Idea' of Bryce Harper Trade This Winter: 5 Potential Landing Spots, Including the NY Yankees
item.dc:creator: Jasonburgosmma; Jason Burgos
item.description: After a disappointing end to the 2026 season, a prominent MLB insider believes the Philadelphia Phillies will consider trading long-time star Bryce Harper this winter. The Phillies entered this year with the fourth-highest payroll in MLB and big expectations. While they didn’t win the National League East, the hope was that their talent-rich roster could still go on a deep run in the postseason. Unfortunately, despite their best efforts, Philadelphia came up short in their three-game Wild Card s
item.content:encoded:
After a disappointing end to the 2026 season, a prominent MLB insider believes the Philadelphia Phillies will consider trading long-time star Bryce Harper this winter.
The Phillies entered this year with the fourth-highest payroll in MLB and big expectations. While they didn’t win the National League East, the hope was that their talent-rich roster could still go on a deep run in the postseason. Unfortunately, despite their best efforts, Philadelphia came up short in their three-game Wild Card series against division rivals the Atlanta Braves.
Following their season-ending loss on Thursday, The Athletic’s Ken Rosenthal claimed, “The Phillies at least need to kick around the idea of trading” the All-Star first baseman. A player the MLB insider feels doesn’t have an “oppressive” contract, with five years and $118 million left on the deal.
If the team pulled the trigger on a trade for the two-time NL MVP this winter, here are five teams he could end up landing with this winter.
Chicago Cubs
The Chicago Cubs had an equally frustrating finish to their 2026 campaign this week as well. However, they didn’t even get to three games, and the team with the sixth highest payroll in baseball was soundly beaten by the San Diego Padres in just two.
Chicago could lose both of their corner outfielders this winter, so Harper could fill either of those spots. Or the nine-time All-Star could be an option at DH. Either way, Harper would be a really nice addition to the lineup. Plus, like Alex Bregman, he is a strong veteran leader and player in the postseason.
Boston Red Sox
The Boston Red Sox are another team that saw their playoff run ended in just two games. In their case, it was rivals the New York Yankees who eliminated them. Harper could certainly be an option for Boston at DH. But the thing this team lacks the most, which he would address, is a proven veteran leader on the field and in the clubhouse. If he can handle the pressure of Philadelphia, Harper would be fine in Boston.
Toronto Blue Jays
This season was a massive disappointment for the Toronto Blue Jays. After being a couple of outs away from winning the World Series last fall, the Jays finished dead last in the AL East with a 79-83 record this year. So you can bet they will look to make a big move this offseason to get back into title contention in 2027.
If the Phillies actually make Harper available in trade talks, Toronto will be fascinated by the idea of pairing him with Vladimir Guerrero Jr. next season. If Guerrero Jr. can return to the player he always has been in 2027, and Kazuma Okamoto puts up similar power numbers, adding Harper to the batting order gives Toronto a spot in the order you can’t pitch around.
New York Yankees
The Yankees are still in the race to be champions in 2026. However, if they fall short of that yearly goal, the Yanks will surely look into adding a piece or two that can get them to end their 17-year title drought.
New York would need to find a new home for Giancarlo Stanton, but with only one guaranteed season for $15 million left on his deal, it may be possible this offseason. If they can trade the injury-prone five-time All-Star, a lineup with a healthy Aaron Judge, Harper, Ben Rice, and Cody Bellinger is one of the best in baseball.
St. Louis Cardinals
While the St. Louis Cardinals finished 77-85 this season, they seemed a bit ahead of schedule in their rebuild because of the upside in young stars JJ Wetherholt and Jordan Walker. The Cards are willing to make bold moves for proven stars if they feel they can help get the team to the next level or change the culture for the better. Harper could do both.
With St. Louis having a top-five farm system in MLB, they would certainly have the prospect assets to easily get a deal done.

item.content:encoded:
The season for the Houston Astros came to an unceremonious close at the hands of the Chicago White Sox, who beat them two games to none in the MLB Wild Card Playoff round.
Now, the White Sox move on to face the divisional rival Cleveland Guardians in the Divisional Playoff round, while the Astros are left picking up the pieces and wondering where things went wrong.
Not long afterward, starter Hunter Brown expressed his frustration with how things turned out in a completely blunt recap.
Houston Astros Pitcher Hunter Brown Admits The Tough Truth After Series Loss To White Sox
Brown's start in Game 2 against the White Sox ended before the first inning was over, forcing the Astros to turn to their bullpen early. The Astros had already utilized eight pitchers during their Game 1 setback, and they also used six more in their regular season finale.
Brown faced nine Chicago batters, allowing five hits and four runs, three of which were earned. He also walked one batter and while also not getting much help from his teammates. The Astros committed a pair of costly errors, while Yordan Alvarez failed to catch a playable fly ball.
Ultimately, the White Sox picked up a 7-3 win, sweeping the Astros out of the playoffs and ending their dreams of another World Series run.
Afterward, Brown said that his performance wasn't up to snuff despite his best efforts.
"I feel like everything that could have went poorly did and I didn't overcome the whole inning, really," Brown said, per Brian McTaggart of MLB.com. "I felt like, looking back, it's hard to say I don't take anything back, but I feel like pitches that I threw I was confident and I threw them to the best of my ability. Just didn't come out on the right end of it. Unfortunately, that's the way it went, and they were able to slap a crooked number up there on the board."
A shoulder strain limited Brown's availability during the 2026 regular season, which saw him finish with a 3.19 ERA in 20 starts.
Hunter Brown Has Played His Entire MLB Career With The Astros
Brown was taken by the Astros in the fifth round (166th overall pick) of the 2019 MLB Draft. After making his professional debut that year, he missed the entire 2020 minor league season before moving through Double-A and Triple-A in 2021.
Brown broke out in 2022 with Triple-A Sugar Land, posting a 2.55 ERA and 106 innings while earning PCL Pitcher of the Year honors. His performance also made him Houston's top prospect and one of MLB's most highly regarded young pitchers.
Brown helped Houston win the 2022 World Series before becoming a full-time starter in 2023. After a strong second half in 2024, he broke out in 2025 with a 2.43 ERA, 206 strikeouts and his first All-Star selection.

item.title: [PhillyVoice] This era of the Phillies feels like it's over
item.dc:creator: Nick Tricome PhillyVoice Staff

item.content:encoded:
October 02, 2026
Ryan Howard twisted uncomfortably out of the batter's box, then crumpled just a few steps down the first-base line as the St. Louis Cardinals rushed toward the mound to celebrate.
An October-fueled Citizens Bank Park fell silent.
The Phillies had lost Game 5 of the 2011 NLDS, and suddenly, shockingly, their all-in chase after another World Series title was over.
Roy Halladay, with his last bit of true greatness, tossed a one-run gem that should've been enough of a chance, and yet was nullified by an even more brilliant complete game from Chris Carpenter, who made a Philadelphia lineup flush with high-profile bats look entirely pedestrian.
And then there was Howard at the end, the star slugger who was left lying there in the grass as the Phillies' grand ambitions all came crashing down.
No one wanted to say it out loud at the time. Maybe they just couldn't bring themselves to fully accept it just yet. But that image has since been permanently etched into the minds of every Phillies fan who witnessed it, because deep down, everyone knew right then and there: A golden era of Phillies baseball was over.
One by one, the generation defined by Howard, Jimmy Rollins, Chase Utley, Cole Hamels, that second-ever World Championship in 2008, and then Halladay, Cliff Lee, and any other big name that the organization could get its hands on in the pursuit of one more, faded.
Those Phillies were never competitive again.
Bryce Harper whiffed on a low and way, way away slider from Chris Sale that he never had a prayer of hitting, and that Drake Baldwin, behind the plate, never had a prayer of catching.
Harper, slowly and totally unaware, bent down to take his shin guard off, thinking it was strike three and that the inning was over. He never saw the ball spike past Baldwin in the dirt, and go rolling to the backstop. By the time he realized, all he gave was a disinterested jog up the first base line, which did finally end the eighth inning from Baldwin having the time to recover for the throw up to the base.
John Kruk: "RUN!"
Bryce Harper was slow to get out of the box, not realizing strike three had gotten away.
(Via: @MLB) pic.twitter.com/GRcx3VGWtQ
— Foul Territory (@FoulTerritoryTV) October 2, 2026
The Phillies were down, 6-2, in the deciding Game 3 of the 2026 NL Wild Card series, on the road against the rival Atlanta Braves.
They still had three outs of life left, but everyone watching knew full well – and probably had no hesitation admitting this time, just shy of 15 years later – that another playoff era of Phillies baseball was over.
And once this club does get back to South Philadelphia, there will be no World Series pennant to look up at in center field and over Ashburn Alley.
The closest this generation ever got was that first breakout run that burnt out against the Astros in 2022.
They only ever got further away from it from there, and now might be all out of chances.
The Phillies stood in the visiting clubhouse, and interim manager Don Mattingly sat at the press conference dais.
No one spoke with any certainties.
Mattingly, who took over midseason for Rob Thomson, talked around whether he wanted to come back and how he felt about the decision the Phillies will have to make this winter for whoever their next full-time manager is going to be.
"It's not the time to talk about anything like that," Mattingly said. "...I want the Phillies to do what they need to do."
Granted, anything shy of a World Series always seemed to point toward him not staying.
Alec Bohm, the first-round and homegrown infielder who was good but always had better expected of him, is now headed for free agency and didn't want to talk about what his future held either.
Trea Turner, who certainly will be back just by the nature of his enormous 11-year, $300 million contract, knows he can't with another season like this one, where his numbers at the plate are low and where you can never be fully confident that he'll properly field the baseball. That can't cut it.
"[I] got a lot of work to do," Turner said.
And then there was Harper, who didn't have much to offer either, save for one definitive statement.
"I'd imagine this team's gonna look a lot different next year," said Harper, "with the guys that are kind of leaving this clubhouse. We'll see."
If there even is a next year for baseball.
Either way, it does feel like this team has to be.
The next few weeks are undoubtedly going to put the Phillies and everyone responsible for their current construction up to harsh scrutiny, amid a fan base that, really, got tired of them two postseason failures ago.
Dave Dombrowski, the Phillies' president of baseball operations, will have the most to answer for, after he repeatedly ran it back with an aging core, failed once again to put together a competent bullpen, and ended this season with none of his trade deadline acquisitions on the postseason roster, all while presiding over a barren-looking farm system.
Hitting coach Kevin Long, who has long been immune from any other shifts in the dugout staff around him, has to face the music here, too, after the Phillies continued to have a collectively abysmal approach at the plate – outside of a month – and after seeing nearly all of the Phils' batters either plateau, regress, or in the case of Luis Arráez, to see a perennial .300-plus hitter suddenly drop well below that line the second he put on a red-pinstriped uniform.
And then there's Harper, the big face of an era that kept falling short and now might not even be good enough to get there to begin with anymore.
All offseason and into spring training, it was clear he was miffed by Dombrowski openly questioning to the press last fall whether he could be "elite" anymore.
Harper said back in February that it wasn't something to motivate him, but he made it obvious, too, that those remarks stuck in his craw.
And he would go on to put up solid numbers, and yeah, he even had his heroics in a Game 2 that kept the Phillies alive for another day.
But now they're done. This era might be done, and with its end forever tied to that moment of Harper leisurely taking his shin guard off at the plate, not knowing the ball went rolling, and by the time he did, not having enough care to even try to fully run it out.
It felt a lot like Ryan Howard 15 years ago. It felt like an era was over.
This one, though, might be a bit more bitter.

item.dc:creator: Safeer MS
item.description: Former Chicago Cubs infielder Anthony Rizzo criticized the Philadelphia Phillies for using Aaron Nola as the starter for Game 3 of the National League Wild Card Series.
